items.title: The Supreme Court is about to decide whether to gut countless federal laws
items.summary:
Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch, left, and Chief Justice John Roberts on the steps of the Supreme Court in 2017 in Washington, DC. | Win McNamee/Getty Images 

Nearly five decades ago, in Cannon v. University v. Chicago (1979), the Supreme Court held that Title IX, the federal law forbidding most schools from engaging in sex discrimination, could be enforced by private plaintiffs filing individual lawsuits against those schools. It was an important decision, because without it, Title IX would be a much weaker law that would only function when the federal government charges someone with violating it.

The Court has since reaffirmed its decision in Cannon at least four times , provided that the plaintiff alleges intentional discrimination. And yet, on November 30, the Supreme Court will hear Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia , a case that asks whether Title IX’s prohibition on sex discrimination may be enforced by through such individual lawsuits. 

The fact that this Court took up a legal question that the Supreme Court has already answered many times is an ominous sign for victims of sex discrimination — and potentially for millions of other individuals whose rights to education, healthcare, and numerous other essentials are protected by federal law. The best case scenario for civil rights plaintiffs is that the justices simply hand down a sixth decision reaffirming a longstanding right, and the worst case scenario could render countless federal laws unenforceable.

Crowther involves a highly technical, but extremely important legal…
items.t: The Supreme Court is about to decide whether to gut countless federal laws

items.title: Connecting with Britain’s unsung carers has allowed me to feel a deep compassion for my younger self | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
items.summary:
Looking after my brother when I was a child was challenging and life-affirming. Now we need to give the next generation of carers proper support

As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives.

There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. If you stood in a busy street in any town or city and stopped a passerby to ask them about the care they’ve given, or indeed the care they have received, many people would have a story to tell.

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnist

items.title: You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?
items.summary:
Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form . Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity: 

My husband and I are not religious. He’s from an Episcopalian family and grew up in the Unitarian Universalist church, and I grew up attending an interdenominational church, but we don’t attend services now. Lately, though, he’s become so anxious about AI safety and the possibility of human extinction that he’s been having trouble sleeping. In the wake of all this existential uncertainty, he’s expressed a renewed interest in attending church. And he’s not interested in the UU church (with its believe-what-you-want attitude); he said he needs “the strong stuff.” 

It’s all a bit mystifying to me because he does not believe in God. But I want him to feel better, and I don’t know what I or anyone can say about AI that will help him manage his anxiety. If religion is what he needs to find solace in the face of radical uncertainty, I want to support him. That said, I have misgivings about attending church myself and about us attending with our kids. I feel a bit self-conscious about being interlopers, and I also feel weird about him going alone every single weekend. More significantly, I wish I understood what the allure is for him. He says he’s hoping it will help him make peace with the end.…
items.t: You’re anxious about AI. Can religion help — even if you don’t believe in God?

items.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause
items.summary:
Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con?

‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live, billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee.

The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. (Fungi are big news in the menopause wellness world, often touted as an answer to brain fog. Though at best the scientific jury is still out, Ocado searches for lion’s mane mushrooms more than…
items.t: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause

items.title: Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.
items.summary:
“When we're playing with a toy, we're often doing something we've never done before, because play is a space where experimentation and risk-taking and mistakes happen,” Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, tells Vox’s Explain It to Me podcast. | Chen Siyumeng/Xinhua via Getty Images 

Recently, I was out doing some window shopping with one of my friends. We checked out some of our usual places — a makeup store, a clothing store — but the place where my friend’s eyes really lit up was a toy store. There were floor-to-ceiling displays of Labubus and Funko Pops, Jellycats that looked like croissants, and just about every Hello Kitty product you could imagine. 

What really got my attention about the space was not the sheer volume of toys, but the lack of kids. It was mostly people our age, with the same excitement that I saw in my friend. This makes sense when you look at a breakdown of the current toy market: It’s an industry projected to be worth over $130 billion worldwide this year, and as of this summer, American adults with no kids bought more games and toys than households with children. There’s even a name for grownups who aren’t ready to put away the toybox: kidults. 

According to Mia Sundstrom, CEO of the National Institute for Play, there’s a reason for our enduring fondness for toys. “The drive to play is actually biologically hardwired into our subcortex,” she told Vox. “Because of that subcortical location, the drive to play actually lasts across the entire lifespan, which means that we’re never too old to play. But our society deeply…
items.t: Adults are buying more toys than ever. You should too.

items.title: Is Raphael Warnock running for president?
items.summary:
Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA) has kept the door open on a presidential bid. | Finn Gomez/Getty Images 

The 2026 midterm elections were less than three weeks ago — and the new Democratic congressional majorities chosen by voters are still more than a month from taking office — but if the 2028 Democratic presidential primary isn’t fully underway, then at the very least, potential candidates are already starting to jockey for position. 

Some of that maneuvering was on display earlier this month at the fittingly named “What’s Next” political conference in Denver. The conference drew Democratic operatives, strategists, and presidential hopefuls from around the country — and Vox’s America, Actually podcast, where host Astead Herndon asked attendees for their thoughts about Democratic Party’s future. 

Herndon also sat down with one possible 2028 candidate: Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA). His background is especially relevant after the midterms: He’s the senior pastor at the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta at a time when more Democratic candidates are embracing religious appeals ; and he’s a student of the civil rights movement, the legacy of which could be seen in surging Black turnout across the South after the Supreme Court rolled back parts of the Voting Rights Act. 

Warnock has kept the door open on a presidential bid ; his colleague Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) is also frequently discussed as a potential candidate .

Herndon and Warnock discussed how Democrats can win in the South following election victories by Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom and others; why Warnock…
items.t: Is Raphael Warnock running for president?

items.title: The strange, thankless job Chris Van Hollen wants to take from Chuck Schumer
items.summary:
Chuck Schumer (D-NY) looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) speaks during a news conference at the Capitol on February 2, 2023. | Drew Angerer/Getty Images 

Sen. Chuck Schumer has led the Senate Democratic caucus for 10 years, and he’s now facing the most serious challenge to his post that he’s ever encountered.

Just as Democrats are about to take their largest majority since the beginning of Barack Obama’s presidency, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Schumer for the role of leading that new majority. Van Hollen has won the backing of several senators so far, as well as various outside progressive groups .

In one sense, the reasons Democrats might want to move on from Schumer are obvious. Schumer is 75 years old, and is not a particularly charismatic messenger or compelling speaker. His personal positions on issues like US support for Israel , and his longtime cultivation of Wall Street and corporate donors, put him out of step with the Democratic base. And polls regularly show that he is extremely unpopular .

At the same time, the job of Senate majority leader also isn’t really about winning a national popularity contest. It’s about leading the Senate — a challenging remit that involves a multitude of tasks, including but not limited to setting the legislative calendar, crafting legislative and big-picture policy strategy, dealing with outside interest groups, coordinating with the speaker of the House and president, and trying to hold the majority in the next election.

And there’s another underappreciated part of the job: volunteering to be the one…
items.t: The real reason Senate leaders keep becoming incredibly unpopular

items.title: Why everyone, even the GOP, is sick of JD Vance
items.summary:
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance at a Veterans Day in Arlington National Cemetery on November 11, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

Remember two weeks ago, when Vice President JD Vance was having a bad week ? It’s gotten much, much worse. 

Vance has spent most of the last two years as the MAGA movement’s heir apparent — so much so that Secretary of State Marco Rubio, potentially his top rival for the 2028 GOP presidential nomination, told a reporter last year that “If JD Vance runs for president, he’s going to be our nominee, and I’ll be one of the first people to support him.”

Suffice to say, that no longer looks like the case: Vance, more than any other potential Republican candidate in 2028, emerged from the midterms in bad political shape, and President Donald Trump has been putting him through hell ever since. 

Specifically, Vance has found himself in a trap of his own making on two issues: The Iran war and immigration. items.title: America’s most visited national park right now is inside GTA VI
items.summary:
In Grand Theft Auto IV, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades. | Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive 

There are plenty of reasons to be excited for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, which came out today. There are the heists, the incredibly realistic depictions of Florida , the surprisingly deep romance , and, you know, the car theft. It’s been 13 years since the last installment of the incredibly popular game series — basically an eternity in 2026 terms.

But personally, I’m interested in the pelicans in flight at sunset and the green scales of an iguana in the street, as seen in the game’s second trailer . There are more than 170 animals in the game, like alligators, manatees, and frogs. There are also 62 species of birds, and players can pull out binoculars and record them all in a logbook. 

Now I’m not a video game writer. I write about biodiversity. So this stuff is basically catnip for me, and I’m not the only one. There are Reddit threads full of excited birdwatchers who are saying that crime sprees will come second to birding in the new game, or that they want to get one of the game’s protagonists, Lucia, some cute birding outfits. The top comment in the New York Times’s review of the game says, “my roommate gets to play the actual game. I get to find all 67 [sic] species of birds. Truly a game for everyone.”

While most of the game takes place in Vice City, which is developer Rockstar’s take on Miami, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades and…
items.t: Come to GTA VI for the crime spree. Stay for the manatee.

items.title: Teachers are reeling from an existential crisis. You’re probably feeling it too.
items.summary:
Braxton Wimbley was crying every day. Her fifth year of elementary school teaching at a public school in Indiana was, by far, her hardest. It was 2022, the first full academic year without Covid restrictions, and her fourth-graders’ social skills were “pretty much nonexistent,” she told Vox. “Because they had spent so much time at home doing whatever they want to do, [they] didn’t have structure and didn’t know when a teacher tells you no, that means no,” Wimbley, now 29, said.

Her students’ parents weren’t much help. Wimbley could see their exhaustion and empathized with the intensity of spending so much time with their kid during the pandemic. “I had parents blaming me for their child’s reading level, their child’s inability to do basic math, and I mean everything,” she said. One parent blamed her for the fact that her fourth-grader read at a kindergarten level. “I was like, ‘That’s not my fault.’”

Right before spring break, Wimbley wrestled with whether this career she had felt called to — growing up, she idolized Miss Honey from Matilda — was even right for her anymore. It was a painful thing to consider. And then a few days later, she was punched by a student. “After that, I was like, ‘Okay, I’m done. This is it,’” Wimbley said. Physically, she was unharmed. Her emotional state was another story.

Why I reported this 

A few years ago, one of my best friends left her job as a middle-school math teacher. For nearly a decade, she’d loved it — and, as her friend, I found her extremely suited to the job. After the pandemic, however, she decided to make a pivot into a…
items.t: Teachers are reeling from an existential crisis. You’re probably feeling it too.

items.title: Barns full of birds from America’s biggest foie gras company just burned down
items.summary:
As this photo from the Monticello Fire Department captured, a sprawling fire burned down several barns at Hudson Valley Foie Gras, America’s largest foie gras producer. | Monticello Fire Department 

Early Thursday morning in upstate New York, a fire broke out at Hudson Valley Foie Gras — the largest US producer of foie gras. French for “fatty liver,” foie gras is a delicacy product that’s made by force-feeding ducks in the final weeks of their lives. 

The fire destroyed multiple barns, and while hundreds of young ducks and geese survived, it’s still unknown how many died. Commercial duck farms tend to house thousands of animals — and sometimes over 10,000 animals — per barn.

“The fire took off so fast, there was no way to get inside to stop the spread,” Charlie Kalinowski, chief of the Smallwood/Mongaup Valley Fire Department, told Radio Catskill.

Approximately 200 first responders from 37 fire departments responded to the blaze, and no humans were injured. Hudson Valley Foie Gras didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, though a vice president at the company told Radio Catskill that they suspect it started due to an electrical malfunction, which hasn’t been confirmed by local fire officials. 

Allie Granger of the nonprofit Animal Welfare Institute told Vox that the cause of barn fires usually goes unreported, but when they are reported, electrical malfunction tends to be among the most common causes at relatively large operations like Hudson Valley Foie Gras.

This incident is expected to hit the US foie gras supply hard, as Hudson Valley Foie Gras is one…
items.t: Barns full of birds from America’s biggest foie gras company just burned down

items.title: Gen Z is getting nostalgic for the Obama era — with an asterisk
items.summary:
“Millennial optimism exists because Obama won elections so decisively that they had time to hit the club afterward,” Olivia Julianna, a Democratic strategist and content creator, said. | Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images 

Millennial optimism is making a comeback online, thanks to the Democrats’ blue tsunami in this month’s midterm election. Social media is filled with videos, songs, and edits celebrating the midterms and linking the feeling to Barack Obama’s victories and the various cultural signifiers of the time, from indie bands to “ girlboss” CEOs . Many of them are produced by Gen Z users who have little memory of the era themselves. 

To some left-leaning millennials, it’s a teachable moment. On Instagram the day after the election, 37-year-old Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) gave her younger followers a lesson in the roots of “millennial cringe,” that mix of hope and earnestness that Gen Zers often see as cloying and naive.

“Imagine all the seats we flipped last night, that feeling, plus on top of it, electing the first Black president ever. And on top of that, you did it the first time you ever voted? That hits generationally ,” Ocasio-Cortez said . “Like, you are chasing that feeling ever since. And because you did it the first time you ever voted, you’re like, ‘Yeah, we can change the world. Yeah, why not. We did it the first time. Why not just do it again?’”

But while some millennials (including many of the victorious candidates ) might proudly claim this moment as a restoration of their culture — everyone back to Hamilton ! — some of the Gen…
items.t: Gen Z is getting nostalgic for the Obama era — with an asterisk

items.title: Was Anthropic’s record US$81 billion listing a vote of confidence in AI – and what’s next?
items.summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant behind Claude, has just pulled off the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history. The company raised US$81 billion by listing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market, beating the previous all-time record of US$75 billion set by SpaceX earlier this year.

Initially set at $US83, Anthropic’s share price soared to US$111 after its debut, briefly nudging the company’s value past US$2 trillion, before falling again as investors took profits.

The blockbuster stock market listing comes at a nervous moment in the AI sector. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the huge sums of money being poured into the AI boom are justified, and many are reducing their exposure to technology stocks.

Adding to this shakiness has been the shock departure of chipmaker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, following an affair scandal.

Anthropic’s debut certainly sets a benchmark for rival OpenAI,…
items.t: Was Anthropic’s record US$81 billion listing a vote of confidence in AI – and what’s next?

items.title: The most iconic sports film of all time taught us winning isn’t everything: 50 years of Rocky
items.summary:
By all measures, Rocky (1976) is the most successful sport film of all time. Half a century on from its release, the story of small-time boxer Rocky Balboa – who rises to square up against heavyweight champion Apollo Creed — continues to capture our imagination.

Directed by John G. Avildsen, the film won the prestigious Best Picture and Best Directing Oscars in 1977. And the broader franchise, consisting of five sequels and three Creed spin-offs, has generated more than US$1 billion at the global box office.

Rocky resonates because it is the ultimate underdog story. The hero is flawed, yet faithful to his dreams – working to overcome his self-doubt. His final victory is not a boxing title, but in proving his worth.

Standing your ground

items.title: Jimmy Dimly is back and we should treasure him while we can | John Crace
items.summary:
Old-school Tory with a heart wants to make London fun again – just don’t mention Brexit

  • Tories select James Cleverly as candidate for London mayor

Sooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”.

As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024. A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate. Only they never did. The only votes she got were from those who had never…
items.t: Jimmy Dimly is back and we should treasure him while we can | John Crace

items.title: Myanmar genocide ruling is a watershed moment in international justice – with huge ramifications for other cases
items.summary:
The International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not.

The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar.

But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have…
items.t: Myanmar genocide ruling is a watershed moment in international justice – with huge ramifications for other cases

items.title: Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors
items.summary:
Despite the countless books, podcasts, TV miniseries and documentaries, people continue to be fascinated by the fall of Elizabeth Holmes and her health-tech startup Theranos. We are now being offered a new insight into the founder through the much-hyped documentary, You Can See Everything.

The initial drama of the documentary takes places 34 days before Holmes started her 11-year prison sentence for investor fraud in 2023. In our research, we examined how Holmes was presented across promotional materials, tweets, talks and interviews over the ten year period from her initial appearance on the public stage in 2013 to the same period in which the documentary begins.

Valued at around US$9 billion (£7 billion) at its peak in 2014, Theranos claimed to have built a device that could run hundreds of lab tests from just a few drops of blood. Holmes and co-founder Sunny Balwani hid that the device could not in fact do what they said, leading to its 2018 shutdown and their convictions for investor fraud (and, in Balwani’s case, defrauding patients as well).

For many, the fascination in Holmes’s story lies in the hubris and deception…
items.t: Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors

items.title: African glamour: the bold women who styled, wrote and read Drum magazine
items.summary:
Drum magazine was an African institution in the 1950s and 1960s. Launched in South Africa, it would go on to publish five regional pan-African editions across eight countries.

Much has been made of the male reporters of the magazine, but a new open source book considers how women used it to shape their worldviews and opportunities. We spoke with media scholar Wanjirũ G. Mbure about Out For Glamour In Africa.

What was Drum?

Initially known as The African Drum, Drum magazine started in South Africa in 1951, three years after apartheid was signed into law. The system of white minority rule would violently disenfranchise Black South Africans.

This was particularly evident in cities like Johannesburg, where large numbers of Black South Africans migrated from rural areas to work on mines. With little investment in housing and social services, they were forced to live on the outskirts of the city.

Magazines thrived in this period, looking to appeal to growing European and African urban consumers. Drum’s founder, South…
items.t: African glamour: the bold women who styled, wrote and read Drum magazine

items.title: Cop31: the world is heading for climate ‘overshoot’ – the UN summit must start planning for what comes next
items.summary:
A surprising thing has happened at the UN climate conference, Cop31, as it gears up to its conclusion in Antalya, Turkey. Negotiators are discussing how to cool the planet.

You might think this should not be surprising, but how to respond to the latest climate science was not on the agenda when the meeting started. Now, the summit’s latest draft decision explicitly recognises a role for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) alongside deep emissions cuts. This is a significant shift, driven by pressure from some of the countries most vulnerable to climate change – the small island states – in response to two alarming scientific reports in the last month.

The World Meteorological Organization has confirmed that the rate at which the Earth is heating up is accelerating. One reason is the planet is becoming less “reflective”: the loss of ice and snow, changes in cloud formation and (paradoxically)…
items.t: Cop31: the world is heading for climate ‘overshoot’ – the UN summit must start planning for what comes next
